vignette:
He is 32, European, married, and works as a private tutor, moving most days between family homes, library study rooms, and the quiet corner tables of cafés where he helps teenagers prepare for exams. Before the stalking began, he likes the rhythm of that work: the careful planning, the one-to-one contact, the satisfaction of watching a student understand something that had seemed impossible an hour earlier. He thinks of himself as patient, reliable, and easy to talk to. He and his wife have a small, ordinary life that had felt steady.

The first contact seems almost forgettable. A parent of a former student sends repeated messages thanking him for the help he gave her son and asking whether he can take on more sessions. At first he responds politely and briefly. When he says his schedule is full, the messages continue. They become more personal, oddly familiar in tone, as if a closeness exists that he does not feel. She comments on his appearance, asks where he is teaching that day, and sends messages late at night. He stops replying, hoping silence will end it.

Instead, her presence begins to enter his daily life. She appears outside the sixth-form college where he has just finished tutoring, standing across the road as if waiting for someone. He tells himself it might be coincidence, but then he sees her again near a café where he often meets students, and later near his flat. She sends emails mentioning places he has been that day and what he was wearing. Reading them, he feels a physical jolt, as though the boundary between his thoughts and the outside world has been broken. He begins checking over his shoulder while teaching, losing his train of thought in the middle of an explanation he has given hundreds of times before.

His wife is the first person to say clearly that this is not just strange, but frightening. By then he is sleeping lightly and waking to every sound from the street. If his phone vibrates, his stomach drops before he even looks at the screen. He starts saving screenshots, logging dates, changing routes. He tells students' parents he has to move sessions online or alter meeting places at short notice, giving vague excuses about scheduling. He hates how evasive he sounds. Tutoring depends on trust and calm; now he arrives scanning windows and parked cars, noticing who is standing too long by a gate, who has walked past twice, which vehicles are unfamiliar.

One afternoon, after finishing a lesson at a student's house, he finds a note tucked under his windscreen wiper. It refers to something he said during the session, something she could only know if she had been nearby listening or watching. He says later that this is the moment the fear settles fully into him. Until then, part of him keeps trying to explain it away. After the note, he feels hunted. He reports her to the police, and though people around him are supportive, he is surprised by how ashamed he feels. He worries others will think he has encouraged it, failed to manage it, exaggerated it. He is especially uneasy because his work requires access to homes and regular contact with families; he begins to fear that his professional life is now contaminated by danger.

As the months go on, his world shrinks. He stops taking on new students. He avoids tutoring in person unless absolutely necessary. When he does go out, he leaves early to circle the block and check whether anyone is waiting nearby. In cafés, he chooses seats facing the door. If a woman with a similar coat or hairstyle walks in, his heart starts racing so fast he can barely hear what his student is saying. At home, he keeps curtains closed and becomes preoccupied with whether doors are locked. His wife notices that he no longer relaxes into evenings the way he used to. Even when they are watching television, he is only partly there, listening for footsteps outside or the buzz of his phone.

Sleep brings little relief. He has vivid dreams in which he is being watched through windows or followed through streets he cannot get out of. He wakes drenched in sweat and sometimes gets up to check each room of the flat. In the daytime, memories intrude without warning: the sight of her across the road, the note under the windscreen, the messages describing his movements. He tries to push them away, but that effort seems only to make them sharper. He becomes irritable in ways that embarrass him. A delayed text from his wife can send him into panic; an unexpected knock at the door can leave him trembling.

He says he misses the version of himself who could move through the world without calculating risk. He still tutors, because work gives shape to the week and because he cares about his students, but it now takes enormous effort. He prepares lessons meticulously yet struggles to concentrate while delivering them. He is constantly torn between wanting life to return to normal and no longer trusting what "normal" means. Even now, with formal contact from the stalker stopped, his body behaves as if the threat is still just outside the frame, waiting for him to forget and let his guard down.
